item.passage:
Transcript: M: Hi. The man at the door said to find the person who organizes the volunteers. Is that you?
W: That's me. You must be Colm. Thanks for signing up. Doors open at ten, so we've got about twenty minutes. Today I'd like you on the welcome table, right by the front door.
M: Oh. I was kind of hoping to help with repairs. I fixed my sister's hair dryer last week. A wire inside the plug had come loose.
W: Nice work. But you have to be sixteen to use the soldering irons. That's our insurance rule, not mine.
M: I'll be sixteen in March, though. Couldn't I just stand next to Mr. Dunmow and pass him tools?
W: Sorry, not even that. Under-sixteens can't be at the electronics table at all. If you're still keen, come and find me in March.
M: OK, fair enough. So what does the welcome table actually do? Just say hello?
W: A lot more than that. Last month nobody was on it, and people stood in the hall for over an hour. Some of them gave up and took their things home again.
M: Wow. That's a long time.
W: So you'll ask each person what's broken, write it on a ticket and send them to the right table. Clothes go to the sewing table by the window. Lamps, radios and anything with a plug go to Mr. Dunmow.
M: What about bikes? My neighbour said she might bring hers.
W: No bikes today. The man who fixes them is away, so just tell people to come back on the fourteenth.
M: Got it. And what if one table gets really busy?
W: Then don't let people stand around. Give them a time to come back and write it on the back of their ticket.
M: That makes sense. Should I ask Mr. Dunmow about watching him at lunch, then? Like, just watching?
W: Ask him yourself. He doesn't get here till half past ten, though.
M: OK. Where are the tickets?
W: In a blue box in the storeroom, next to the extension cables. Could you go and get them now and set up before the doors open?
M: Sure, I'll go now.

item.prompt: What does the woman say about her own courses at university?
item.passage:
Transcript: W: Hi! Can you see me now? I had to sit by the window to get a signal.
M: Yeah, I can see you. Your room looks tiny.
W: It is tiny, but I like it. So, Mum said you wanted to ask me something.
M: Right. Well, you're not using your bedroom anymore, so I was thinking I could move into it. It's twice the size of mine.
W: Hold on. I'm coming home for the winter break in six weeks. Where would I sleep?
M: In my room. It's only for three weeks.
W: Your room smells like football boots. Anyway, why do you suddenly need more space?
M: I'm choosing my courses for next year, and I want to take the advanced art course. You have to do a big painting at home, and there's no space for an easel in my room.
W: Advanced art? Last month you told me you were taking extra physics.
M: I changed my mind. My art teacher thinks my drawings are good enough, and I'd rather paint than do physics problems.
W: Well, I nearly made the same mistake here at university. I picked chemistry because Dad wanted me to, and I dropped it after the first week. Now I'm doing history of art, and I love it.
M: So you agree with me?
W: About the course, yes. About my room, I'm not sure. All my books are still on the shelves.
M: I could put them in boxes. I'd be really careful.
W: You broke my lamp the last time you were really careful.
M: That was two years ago! I'm a much better brother now.
W: OK, OK. What about the corner of the living room? Nobody uses it since Dad moved the piano.
M: Mum would never let me put paint near the sofa.
W: True. Look, let's not decide tonight. When I'm home in December, I'll look at both rooms, and we'll talk to Mum together.
M: Fine. But don't tell her about the lamp.

She gave up a subject her father chose and prefers the one she took instead
She picked chemistry because her dad wanted it and still enjoys it
She chose history of art first because her dad wanted her to
